opener.heading: Week 11: St. Patrick's Day & Springtime Beginnings 🍀
about: Spring starts on the windowsill. Azlyn scatters cress seed onto wet cotton balls on Friday morning and cuts it for sandwiches on Thursday, and in the days between she plants a potato that stays in its bucket until summer, fills twelve egg-box cups with twelve things off the sidewalk, and builds a nest out of twigs and torn fleece. All of it stays where she walks past it, so she checks on it without being asked.

St. Patrick's Day lands on Wednesday and takes the whole day. A leprechaun trap holds the end of the table from breakfast until bedtime, and soda bread goes in the oven at one and comes out warm before three. Friday's Around the World page covers that loaf, which puts the sour-milk trick in her hands five days before Wednesday needs it.
azlyn: What a seed needs. One cress pot on the sill and one shut in a dark cupboard, opened side by side on Thursday.
Sorting to a rule she invented. Twelve finds in twelve numbered cups, and she says out loud what makes a pile a pile.
Building a shape that holds. Twigs on the outside, grass in the gaps, the softest thing pressed into the middle.
Wet and dry. How much water turns soil into soup and how much turns it into cake, then the same question again in a bread bowl.
Catching with her arms. A scarf falls slow enough for her to get both hands under it, and the ball is that same skill at speed.
you: Novelty is a genuine intervention, not a frivolity
Collecting and categorizing peaks around now
Sick days need less input, not more
Play is how children process what's happened to them
The best activity is the one you have energy for
A play structure that stays up gets richer, not staler
Catching is harder than it looks, and slower is the fix

opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 9 months this week. He pulls to stand on anything at the right height, closes thumb and finger on things the size of a seed, and waves at people in the street.

days.title: Seeds on the Windowsill
days.prepTonight: The lima bean has been soaking since last night. Stand the empty bottles, the cotton balls and the cress seeds by the sink, and cut a dry sponge into squares for Kreston.

opening.title: The Plant Inside the Bean
opening.need: the soaked lima bean · 1 dry bean from the packet · 1 saucer.
steps: Put the two beans side by side on the saucer. She presses each one and finds that a night in water turned a stone soft.
Slide your thumbnail into the soaked one and open it into two halves. A small pale plant lies down the middle, root and first leaves already formed.
Hold it to the window and let her find the pointed end. Tell her the bean going into the jar at 9:15 sits against the glass, so she can watch that root come out.

main.title: The Windowsill Garden
materials: 1 packet cress seeds (or dried lentils or mung beans, which sprout in the same few days)
1 tray to stand the pots on
steps: Cut the bottles down to about the height of her hand. You hold the scissors and she holds the bottle steady.
She packs cotton balls into every pot and wets it from the pitcher until it is soaked, with nothing standing in the bottom.
A pinch of seed on top of each, scattered and left on the surface. Some pots get far too many. Leave them.
Fill one last pot the same way and shut it in a dark cupboard. That one gets water and no light, and she cuts both on Thursday.
For the jar, curl a strip of paper towels inside against the glass, wedge the soaked bean between paper and glass halfway down, and pour water two fingers deep into the bottom.
Tape a label to every pot. She says what it should say, you write her words, and the row goes on the sunniest sill with the tray underneath.
main.tip: Cress shows green in three days and is ready in five. Top the jar up each morning and let her check the water line.

outside.title: Hunting the First Green
paras: Walk the usual route with one job: find green. Mid-March gives you daffodil spears against walls, crocus going over, and forsythia breaking yellow along the fences. Count her finds on your fingers and stop at the first tree with fat buds.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and has the pincer grip now, thumb and finger closing on anything the size of a seed. Give him a shallow tray of dry sponge squares, each one wider than his mouth, to pick up and drop well away from the seed packet. On the walk, hold a grass stem or a bare twig out for him to grab and pull, and keep hold of your end. The daffodils are Azlyn's to look at and nobody's to pick.

second.title: The Potato in a Bucket
second.intro: The cress gets cut and eaten by Thursday. The potato goes in this afternoon and stays in until summer.
materials: 1 bucket or old dishpan with holes punched in the bottom
1 trowel or a big metal spoon
A handful of stones for the bottom
1 strip of masking tape for the label
steps: Find the sprouts on the potato and let her feel them.
Punch the drainage holes yourself, then let her lay the stones over them.
She fills the bucket a third deep with soil. Give her the trowel and expect most of it to arrive by hand.
Sit the potato on the soil with the sprouts pointing up. She chooses the spot, and one potato in a bucket this size is plenty.
Cover it with another hand's depth of soil and press it flat.
Water it until it runs out of the bottom.
Tape the label on, write POTATO, MARCH 12 and her name, and stand the bucket where she walks past it.
second.tip: Once the leaves are tall, pile more soil over them and let her do the piling. Buried stem makes more potatoes.

alternatives: Sow the cress and stop there; the bucket keeps.
Plant into a cut-down milk carton if there is no bucket in the house.
Dig a patch of the yard with no plan and see what comes up.
Sort the stones by size before any of them go in.
outAgain: A friend's house, and take a spare cress pot as a present
The garden center, for the smell of it and the seed racks at her height
The park, for whatever is flowering under the trees
A walk past a yard with a wall low enough to see over
The backyard, watering everything twice

aroundWorld.title: Ireland 🍀
paras: Irish soda bread exists because a damp country with soft wheat needed a loaf that rises without yeast. Baking soda meets sour buttermilk, the mix gives off gas, and the loaf rises in the oven instead of on the counter. Farm kitchens baked it in a covered pot over the fire, and the cross cut across the top let heat reach the middle.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Stir a spoon of lemon juice into milk and leave it five minutes. It thickens and sours, and that is the buttermilk you bake with on Wednesday.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Irish families said the cross was cut to let the fairies out. It also stops a dense loaf staying raw in the center.

days.krestonPM: Sit him on a towel beside the bucket while she digs. At 9 months he pulls to stand on anything solid, so give him an upturned bucket of his own to haul on. A fistful of soil reaches his mouth the second you look away, so keep him at arm's length.

insight.headline: Novelty is a genuine intervention, not a frivolity.
paras: Azlyn's attention runs on how much a thing differs from what she saw yesterday. New input drives the system that tags something as worth watching, and a three-year-old's threshold for new sits low, so a bean split open on a saucer buys you attention the same bean in a packet never would. It explains why she goes fidgety on the seventh reading of a book and why a windowsill that changes on its own holds her for two weeks. A pot she checks every morning, different each time, does the work of a new toy for the price of a seed packet.

days.safety: Cress seeds and soaked beans are the exact size Kreston's new pincer grip was built for, and they scatter across a floor unnoticed. Sweep before he goes down. The scissors stay with you and go back up between cuts. Everybody washes their hands after the soil.

days.title: Twelve Cups to Fill
days.prepTonight: Put two or three egg cartons, the scissors and a marker on the table, and stand the rain boots by the back door with a grocery bag tucked into one of them.

opening.title: Twelve Empty Cups
steps: Cut the lids off the egg cartons so you are left with the trays of cups. She counts them as they come free and you stop the counting at twelve.
Number the cups one to twelve in marker while she watches. She will want to write some herself, so hand the pen over and take whatever comes.
Give her the rule now: twelve cups, twelve things, no two the same. Leave her the rest of the hour to decide where she wants to look first.

main.title: No Two the Same
materials: 2–3 egg cartons, cut into twelve numbered cups
1 grocery bag for wet or muddy finds
steps: Start on the front step. First find goes in cup one.
From there she leads. Yard, curb strip, gutter, the base of the wall, the crack in the sidewalk.
Hold the line on the rule. A second stone goes back down unless she can say what makes it different from the first.
Wet or muddy things go in the grocery bag and rejoin the tray at home. Spares go in the paper bags for the board this afternoon.
By cup nine the easy things have gone. Slow the walk right down. Look up, because bark, catkins and moss all live above the height she searches.
Fill the last cup on the way back to the door, then sit on the step and count the twelve out loud together.
main.tip: Twelve is the number, so keep your hands in your pockets for the last three.

outside.title: Catkins and Sticky Buds
paras: Walk it again with your hands free this time. Find a buckeye or a horse chestnut and put her finger on a sticky bud, a whole leaf packed inside varnish. The willows are in catkin too, gray and furry under her thumb. Break one budded twig off to stand in water at home. She watches it open indoors before the tree outside does.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and waving at people, which on a Saturday street earns him a response from a stranger about every third house. Let that run. Sit him on your lap while Azlyn hunts and give him a wooden block, too big to swallow. The budded twig stays in your hand. He works at surfaces with one finger now, so let him run it over the block and then over the wall you are sitting on. Rough beside smooth gives him two to compare.

second.title: Labels for Everything
second.intro: The twelve cups come indoors and get argued over. She sorts them her way, then your way, then the whole lot goes on a board that hangs up for the week.
materials: 1 large sheet of card, or a flattened cereal box
1 pair of scissors, for the two holes (adult only)
A length of string to hang it
steps: Tip the tray onto the table and let her sort it into piles her own way. Do not name the categories for her.
Ask what each pile is called. Write the name on masking tape and stick it down beside the pile, in her words and not tidied up.
Sort the same twelve again by your rule instead, hard and soft, or living and not living. Say out loud that the piles came out different both times.
Tape the flat things straight to the card and glue the rest. She decides the order they go in.
Under each one, write the label she gives you. The stick with the green on it beats moss twig.
Crayon round the edges, you make two holes with the point of the scissors, she threads the string.
Hang it at her height, low enough that she can put her hand on any of it.
second.tip: Leave four gaps on the board. Anything she finds between now and Thursday goes into them.

alternatives: Sort by color into six lines on the floor and stop there.
Rub crayon over paper laid on the bark and the wall.
Wash every stone in soapy water and see what color they go.
Photograph each of the twelve and let her name them for the picture.
outAgain: The lakeshore, for water birds and the flat stones at the edge
A street you never walk, hunting for finds that are not on yours
The park, for the biggest tree the two of you can reach round
The garden center, warm and full of things in flower
Home and the board, if the morning has already used her up
days.krestonPM: He wants the twelve finds and cannot have them, so give him his own bowl beside the table: a wooden spoon, a plastic lid and a wooden block, all too big to swallow. At 9 months he pulls to stand on a table edge, so anything within a hand's reach of the rim counts as his. Keep the small piles in the middle and the glue lid on.

insight.headline: Collecting and categorizing peaks around now.
paras: Azlyn is at the age where a pocket comes home full of gravel. Sorting things into groups is how she builds the shelves that everything else gets stored on, and the urge to gather runs stronger around three than at any other point in childhood. Sorting twelve stones into piles whose logic nobody else can see means testing a rule she invented and holding twelve items in mind while she does it. Ask her what makes a pile a pile, and take the answer as given. The category matters less than the fact she built one and can tell you why.

days.safety: Spring collecting means bulbs, berries and yew within her reach. Daffodil bulbs are poisonous and so is yew, and both grow in the yards along her route. Nothing she finds goes in a mouth, hands get washed before the snack, and the collection lives off the floor once Kreston is down.

days.title: The Nest Day
days.prepTonight: Tear an old towel or fleece into strips, cut the string into pieces no longer than your hand, and pile both into the cereal bowl on the table.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Nest You Can Sit In

opening.title: Soft, Softer, Softest
opening.need: the torn fabric strips · yarn ends · cotton balls · dry grass or hay · 1 tray.
steps: Lay the materials in a row and let her handle each one with her eyes shut while you name it.
Ask her to put them in order, softest at one end and scratchiest at the other. Take her order even where you disagree.
Tell her a bird makes the same decision every spring, the rough stuff on the outside and the softest thing it can find in the middle. Leave the line where it is.

main.title: The Nest on the Table
materials: Small dry twigs from the yard
1 old towel or fleece torn into strips
String cut into short pieces, nothing longer than a hand
1 hard-boiled egg or a smooth stone
steps: The bowl is the mold and everything gets built inside it.
Twigs first. She bends and pushes them round the inside until they hold each other. Short ones weave and long ones snap.
Dry grass next, wound the same direction, with the short string pieces worked in where the gaps are widest.
Then the soft layer in the order she set at breakfast: cotton balls, yarn ends, fabric strips, pressed down into the middle.
Lift the nest out of the bowl. If it falls apart, she rebuilds it with more grass and fewer twigs.
Test it with the egg. Sit the egg in the hollow and tilt the nest. One that holds the egg on a slope works in a tree.
main.tip: If it will not hold together, wet the grass. Damp grass grips itself, which is why a robin flies mud in.

outside.title: Nests in the Bare Branches
paras: This is the last week you can see into a tree. The leaves are days off, and last year's nests still sit up there in plain view. Walk with your heads back and hunt them. Count how high the highest one is in Azlyns, not in feet. Watch for birds carrying things. A beak with grass in it is going somewhere, so stand still for two minutes.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and has both hands working against each other. Give him his own square of fleece and a folded dish towel on a tray, both too big to swallow, and let him drag and bunch them. The string, the hay and the yarn ends stay out of his reach. On the walk he goes on your front so his head is up where the nests are.

second.title: The Nest You Can Sit In
second.intro: A nest works at any size. Hers is the width of a cereal bowl. The one after lunch takes the corner of the living room and holds all three of you.
materials: 1 laundry basket, or a cleared corner
The afternoon snack and a lidded cup
steps: Clear the corner and set the basket in the middle of it. If the basket is too small for two, work in the corner itself and leave it for Kreston.
Rough stuff on the outside. Cushions stand on their edges in a ring with a gap left for a door.
Blankets go inside, folded and pressed into the base until the floor gives under her feet.
Send her in to test it. She will want it smaller, so pull the cushions in until it fits her.
Move in with the books, the snack and the lidded cup. The afternoon happens in here.
Read one book, then stop talking and let her fill the quiet.
If the light goes, hand her the flashlight and read one more.
second.tip: Get in with her. She built it for three, and an adult who sits down inside stays put longer.

alternatives: One blanket over two chairs, cushions on the floor, done in four minutes.
Line a shoebox with the leftovers and give it to a teddy.
Sit in the nest and go through the bird book.
Stand the small nest on the windowsill beside the cress.
outAgain: A nature hunt walk, listing five things a bird could use and finding them
The park with a bag of yarn ends to tuck into a hedge
A slow loop of the block, counting every bird you can hear
The woods, for moss and the smell of it after rain
Straight back into the indoor nest if the wind is up
days.krestonPM: Put him in the nest. At 9 months a walled space he can sit up in without toppling beats any toy in the house. He will haul himself up on the laundry basket rim, so weight it with a folded blanket and stay in there with him. Loose blankets stay away from his face.

insight.headline: Sick days need less input, not more.
paras: On the morning one of them wakes up wrong, the instinct is to fill the hours with something good enough to make up for it. A small body running a temperature is already working hard, and a new activity is one more thing to process. Use today's nest as the template for those days. One warm contained space, a pile of books, the same three she heard yesterday, and long stretches where nothing is asked of her. Azlyn mends faster with fewer transitions, less noise and you within reach. Keep the food and the fluids, cancel the rest, and let the plan wait.

days.safety: The cut string, the yarn ends, the hay and the twigs go out of reach the moment Kreston is on the floor. Never leave him alone in either nest. Weight the laundry basket with a folded blanket so it cannot come over, and keep loose blankets and cushions clear of his face. The hard-boiled egg has been handled all morning, so it goes in the trash.

days.title: Dinner Made of Mud
days.prepTonight: Drag the crate in from the shed with the saucepan, the sieve and the wooden spoon you can lose to the yard. Freeze the ice-cream tub for tomorrow: water, coloring, the toys dropped in, and a small bottle of water for Kreston.

opening.title: Retiring the Saucepan
opening.need: 1 old saucepan · 1 wooden spoon · 1 sieve · 1 muffin tin · 1 permanent marker.
steps: Lay the utensils out and tell her these ones are leaving the kitchen for good.
Let her mark each handle with the pen, whatever mark she makes.
Ask what she is cooking first on them. Write that answer down too, because at 1:00 she is making it.

main.title: Building the Mud Kitchen
materials: 1 crate, or a sturdy cardboard box
Heavy scissors or a craft knife (adult only)
steps: Stand the crate in the yard where the kitchen will live and check the top against her waist.
Sit the bowl on top and draw round it. Cut a finger inside your line so the rim of the bowl holds it up. Knife back on the shelf between cuts.
Drop the bowl in. That is the sink.
Tape a length of string along the front and clip the clothespins to it. Every utensil now has a place to hang.
Reinforce the corners with packing tape, inside and out, then shove it hard to check it takes her leaning on it.
Write her name down the side in the biggest letters that fit, and let her hang the dish towel.
main.tip: Cardboard gives you a month of this before it goes soft; a crate lasts years. Either way, stand it against a wall so it cannot come over on top of her.

outside.title: Measuring the Puddles
paras: March rain leaves the same puddles in the same places, so adopt three on your usual route for the spring. Push a stick straight down into each one, mark the wet line with your thumb, then stand the stick against her leg. Knee puddle, ankle puddle, toe puddle. Come back tomorrow and see which one shrank. Rain boots, and spare socks in the bag.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and pulls to stand on anything at the right height, so the new counter is a magnet before the tape has settled. Let him haul up on the far end of it while the sink bowl is still dry, with your hand behind him. At ground level he gets the muffin tin and a wooden spoon. He bangs metal on metal with intent now, and it is loud, and it is his.

second.title: The First Mud Dinner
second.intro: The counter is up by lunchtime. She cooks on it this afternoon and on most afternoons between now and October.
materials: Masking tape and 1 permanent marker for the menu
steps: Fill the sink from the pitcher. Two inches, no more, and tip it out the moment either of you walks away.
Give her a bowl of soil and let her find how much water turns it to soup and how much turns it to cake.
Cake first. Mud pressed into the muffin tin, turned out onto a slab, decorated with petals, leaves and grit.
Soup next, in the saucepan, with the sieve as the tool that separates. She will strain the same mud four times to see what stays behind.
Take the order. Sit down at the counter, ask what is on the menu, and eat it with a straight face.
Whatever she names a dish, write it on masking tape and stick it to the front of the counter.
Wash the dishes in the sink in real water and hang everything back on the clothespins. Washing the dishes is the part she asks for tomorrow.
second.tip: Do not correct the recipes. Soup made of grass, one stone and a whole dandelion is a dish.

alternatives: A dishpan of mud on the grass and nothing else.
Cocoa powder and water in a tray indoors if it is too cold out.
Paint the fence with a brush and a bucket of clean water.
outAgain: The woods loop, and bring a bag of ingredients home for the counter
The riverside path, for the sound of water moving fast in March
A route chosen for its puddles, deepest first
The backyard, if she is still cooking and does not want to stop
days.krestonPM: Keep him away from the sink the entire time. Set him on a rug with his own bowl of cooked, cooled pasta and a spoon. At 9 months he passes a fistful from one hand to the other and back, and everything he lifts goes to his mouth first, so give him something he is allowed to eat and sit beside him with a washcloth.

insight.headline: Play is how children process what's happened to them.
paras: Azlyn cooks a dinner and serves it to you because she has watched somebody do that a thousand times and still has questions about it. Pretend play is where she takes an experience apart and reassembles it with herself in charge. Watch what she reenacts, because the scene she keeps coming back to is the one she is working on. A child who plays doctor for two weeks after an appointment is digesting it. The mud kitchen hands her the adult world at her own scale, with real water, real tools and a menu nobody else gets to write. Sit down and order something.

days.safety: Kreston pulls to stand this month and the sink bowl holds enough water to drown him. Tip it out every single time you step away, and never leave him near it. Soil carries what cats and dogs leave behind, so hands get washed before any food. The craft knife is adult-only and goes back up out of reach between cuts.

days.title: The Ice Block
days.prepTonight: The ice block has been in the freezer overnight. Deep tray, old towel and the swim bag by the door.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Sunny Side of the Wall

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: Hanging the Wet Swim Things Up

opening.title: Turning Out the Ice Block
opening.need: the frozen tub · 1 deep tray or roasting pan · 1 old towel.
steps: The ice-cream tub you froze last night holds the ice block, toys and all. Run the outside of the tub under the warm tap for ten seconds and turn the block out into the tray. It lands with a thump she will want repeated.
Let her walk round it and find every object trapped inside. Count them out loud so you both know how many she is going for.
Ask which one comes out first. Take the guess and leave the block in the tray until 9:15.

main.title: Freeing What's Frozen
materials: 1 ice-cream tub of water, frozen overnight with a few drops of food coloring
4–5 objects too big to swallow (a toy car, a plastic dinosaur, a large spoon, a shell)
Table salt in a small dish
1 squeeze bottle or turkey baster (or a second spoon)
steps: Set the tray on the towel on the floor and hand her nothing for the first minute. Hands, breath, banging.
Warm water first, in the squeeze bottle. She aims at one spot and watches a channel drill down through the block.
Salt second. A spoonful sprinkled over the surface, then a wait. Salt eats a pitted, cratered path of its own.
The third method is waiting. Break off a corner, stand it on a saucer on the windowsill, and let it run on its own all morning.
Every few minutes ask which is winning. She calls it and you say her answer back.
Cheer the last object out. Pour the colored meltwater into the pitcher and let her water Friday's potato bucket with it.
main.tip: Warm water, not hot. Straight off the tap it cracks the block into lumps and takes the whole hour with it.

outside.title: The Sunny Side of the Wall
paras: Go and find the difference the sun makes. Put her hand flat on a south-facing wall and then on the shaded side of the same wall. In March she can feel the gap through her palm. Frost sits along the bottom of a shaded wall until lunchtime after a cold night, and a mild morning gives her a dry warm strip and a damp cold one instead. A warm brick wall at her back buys ten more minutes outside.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and the ice block is not for him. A lump that size holds enough cold to hurt his hands. Freeze a small bottle half full of water instead, or a washcloth frozen flat, and sit him on a towel with it while you stay beside him. He turns it over and drops it, and it stays too big to swallow.

second.title: The Paper Rainbow
second.intro: Swimming is at 2:30, so there is no afternoon left for a project with steps. This one gets made on the sofa.
materials: Colored paper, or magazine and junk-mail pages cut into strips
steps: Cut the paper into strips about two fingers wide. She cuts the wonky ones and you cut the rest.
Sort the strips into color piles on the sofa. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple, and one pile for the ones neither of you can name.
Make the first loop and glue it. Show her once, then hand the whole job over.
Thread the next strip through and glue it shut. Once she has three linked she will keep going without you.
Keep the color order running. She will drop a blue into the reds, and it stays where she put it.
Count the loops in tens as you go, and write the total on a strip when she stops.
Thread string through the end loops and tape it up high across the room. It becomes the ceiling over tomorrow's leprechaun trap.
second.tip: Glue stick rather than tape for the loops she makes on her own. Tape needs two hands and a thumb on the join.

alternatives: One color, no sorting, as long a chain as she wants.
Cut the strips today and chain them tomorrow.
Sort the magazine pages into color piles and leave it at that.
outAgain: Swimming
The shallow end and nothing more, if she is running out
The indoor play center, if the pool is shut for a school session
A café with the swim bag still in the car
Home, and the chain gets longer
days.krestonPM: He swims too. At 9 months he sits on the pool step in shallow water with both your hands on him, and he slaps the surface to make the splash come back. Twenty minutes is the whole of it. Get him out while he is still enjoying himself and dry his head first, because that is where the heat goes.

insight.headline: The best activity is the one you have energy for.
paras: Some days this book is a menu and the right choice is the smallest thing on it. A paper chain on the sofa with you sitting beside her does more for Azlyn than an ambitious project you come to resent halfway through, because she reads your state long before she reads the activity. Children take their cue from the adult running it. The plan on this page came off a full night of sleep, and it shows. Cross out the hard one, keep the snack and the walk, and let a low day be a low day. The windowsill grows without either of you watching it.

days.safety: Bare skin comes off the block after the first minute, and it never goes against her face. The salt dish stays with you between spoonfuls. Kreston gets the frozen bottle or the frozen washcloth and never a loose ice cube, and you stay beside him while he has it. Mop the meltwater as it spreads, because he pulls to stand beside the tray. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: The Trap and the Loaf
days.prepTonight: Check you have baking soda and something gold in the house, chocolate coins, buttons or a strip of foil, and stand the shoebox by the table.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Shiniest Things in the House

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: Bread and Butter on the Table

opening.title: The Shiniest Things in the House
opening.need: 1 basket or bowl · kitchen foil · anything gold-colored.
steps: Send her round the house hunting shiny. Coins, buttons, a teaspoon, foil, whatever tinsel survived Christmas.
Sort the basket into gold and everything else.
Tell her the plan now, that a leprechaun cannot walk past gold, and give her the hour to decide where the trap goes.

main.title: The Leprechaun Trap
materials: 1 stick or a pencil to prop it
Chocolate coins, buttons or anything gold-colored
Paper and crayons for the sign
steps: Pick the spot together and clear it. The trap stands there all day, so it goes on a table top or behind a door you can shut, never on the floor while Kreston is loose.
Prop the box on its side on the stick, open end down. Practice the collapse three or four times until she can bring it down on purpose.
Bait underneath. Foil, coins and buttons counted out loud into a small pile in the middle.
Build the ramp from cardboard offcuts and tape it to the box, then add the craft-stick ladder up the far side.
Tie the string to the stick and run it along the table edge to a chair she kneels on. One pull drops the box.
She makes the sign, in her own marks, and you write her words underneath in yours.
main.tip: Build it so she can reset it herself. A trap only you can rebuild gets sprung twice and abandoned.

outside.title: Three Leaves or Four
paras: Clover is up in every lawn and along every curb this week. Get down on the grass with her and look at how the three leaves sit around the stem. Four-leaf clovers turn up about once in five thousand, so the game is how many threes she can check before her patience runs out. Press one good three-leaf in a book on the way in.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and waves at everybody, so walk him along the fence line where the neighbors are. Out on the grass he gets clover to grab and pull with both hands. He pulls to standing on anything solid, so a low wall with your hand behind him beats the stroller for the last ten minutes.

second.title: Soda Bread with No Waiting
second.intro: Bread with no yeast in it and no rising time. She measures it at 1:00 and eats it warm before three.
materials: 400 ml buttermilk (or milk with 1 tbsp lemon juice stirred in and left five minutes, or plain yogurt loosened with milk)
steps: Oven on at 425°F and say out loud that it is on. It stays on for forty minutes.
She tips the flour, the baking soda and the salt into the bowl and stirs them with the wooden spoon.
Buttermilk in all at once. She mixes until no dry flour is left and stops there. Soda bread wants a rough dough and goes tough if it gets worked.
Tip it onto the floured tray and let her push it into a round about as thick as her hand.
She cuts the cross with the table knife, right across and deep, almost to the bottom. Dust flour over the top.
Thirty-five to forty minutes in the oven. Tap the base when it comes out and let her hear the hollow knock.
Butter on the table, sliced warm, and she checks the trap between slices.
second.tip: A heavy loaf means the milk was not sour enough to fire all the soda. It still tastes of butter.

alternatives: Half the mix cut into six rolls, which bake in fifteen minutes.
Buy the bread and spend the whole afternoon on the trap.
Make the ramp, the ladder and the sign and forget the trap.
outAgain: The library (every two weeks), for the Irish picture books that are out this week
The indoor play center, if the library is full of people with the same idea
The store, for one more gold thing to add to the bait
Home to guard the trap, which is a fair answer today
days.krestonPM: Take him to the library and set him in the board-book corner while Azlyn chooses. At 9 months he pulls to standing on the low shelves and hauls the books off them. Let Azlyn pick his. Back home, keep him out of the kitchen while the tray moves, and give him the empty flour bowl and a spoon.

insight.headline: A play structure that stays up gets richer, not staler.
paras: The trap earns its keep by staying in the corner. A thing built and cleared away inside an hour is a craft. A thing left standing becomes a place she keeps returning to, and every return adds something: a better ramp, a second sign, a rule about who is allowed to look. Three-year-olds work in short visits, four minutes at a time across a whole day, and the play gets deeper with each pass. Leave the fort up, leave the trap up, leave the board on the wall. The clutter buys you an afternoon of her going back to it on her own.

days.safety: The oven runs hot for forty minutes and Kreston pulls to stand on whatever is nearest, the oven door included. Keep him out of the kitchen while the tray is moving. Chocolate coins, foil and buttons are choking hazards, so the trap sits on a table top or behind a shut door and the bait gets counted out and counted back in. Run the string along the table edge to the chair she kneels on and never across the floor, and untie it from the stick every time she leaves the trap, because a loose string at Kreston's height is a strangulation risk.

days.title: The Catch and the Cress
days.prepTonight: Boil two eggs and leave them in the fridge, roll three pairs of socks into balls, and put the scissors beside the cress pots on the sill.

opening.title: Three Socks and a Basket
opening.need: 3 rolled sock balls · 1 laundry basket · masking tape.
steps: Tape a line on the floor and stand the basket a stride beyond it.
She throws from the line. Move the basket closer until she gets three out of three, then leave it there.
Swap over. She holds the basket and moves it to catch what you throw.

main.title: Slow Things First
materials: 1 light scarf or a square of thin fabric
2 balloons (or a second scarf, or a paper bag half filled with air)
Masking tape for a line on the floor
steps: Scarf first. Hold it above her head and let go. It takes about two seconds to come down and she has time to get both hands under it.
Ten catches with the scarf before anything else comes out.
Balloon second. It moves like the scarf, only faster, and it bounces off her hands. Throw underhand and high so it arrives from above her.
Paper bag third, half filled with air. It has some weight to it and it still floats down.
Sock ball fourth, from two steps away, thrown to land against her chest. Tell her to hug it, because a three-year-old catches with her arms long before her hands.
Soft ball last. If it will not work today, go back to the scarf and finish on a catch.
main.tip: Say her name, pause, then throw. That pause is what lets her get her hands up.

outside.title: The Wind Takes the Scarf
paras: March wind is the activity. Throw the scarf up where the gusts can get at it and it travels sideways instead of down. Find the corner of a building where the wind funnels and let her stand in it. Drop a handful of dry leaves, watch where they go, then walk over and drop them again.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and cannot catch, but he tracks. Sit him on the floor and drop the scarf onto his head from a hand's height. He pulls it off, you do it again, and that is peekaboo running on his own hands. Balloons stay out of the room while he is down.

second.title: The Sandwich She Grew
second.intro: Six days ago she scattered seed onto wet cotton balls. This afternoon she cuts it with scissors and the house eats it.
materials: The jam-jar bean, for a last look at the root
steps: Bring both pots to the table, the one off the windowsill and the one out of the cupboard, and let her look at the pair before either of you says a word.
Ask what happened to the cupboard one. Take her explanation, give her the word for what the green needs, then stand the pale pot in the light to see whether it comes back.
She cuts the cress, a fistful at a time, holding the top and cutting low.
Mash the eggs with the fork and stir the mayonnaise in. She does the mashing, and it takes longer than you want.
Butter the bread. She spreads, you go round the edges.
Cress on thick, second slice on top, and she cuts them into whatever shape she asks for.
One sandwich for every person in the house, carried to the table by her, with the bean jar brought over so everyone can see how far the root has gone.
second.tip: Cress grows back once from the same pot if the roots stay in and the cotton stays wet. Sow the rest of the packet today and she has a second crop by month's end.

alternatives: Cress on buttered toast cut into fingers, no egg involved.
Cut the lot into a bowl and let everyone grab from it.
Draw the bean, root and all, before it leaves the jar.
Plant the bean out into the potato bucket and see what it does.
outAgain: The market, for a plant of her own to carry home
The produce aisle, and let her buy one thing she cannot name
The park, for kite weather and a scarf in her hand
A walk past other people's front yards, hunting for what is up
The garden center, for seeds for the next round
days.krestonPM: Give him a plate at the table with the crusts and a few strands of cress on it. At 9 months the pincer grip lets him lift a single strand and steer it to his mouth, and cress is soft enough to be safe. He will wear more than he eats. Let Azlyn hand him the plate, since she grew it.

insight.headline: Catching is harder than it looks, and slower is the fix.
paras: Catching asks Azlyn to predict where a moving object will be, get her hands there before it arrives, and close them at the right instant. The timing runs on a nervous system she is still growing, and most three-year-olds catch with their arms and their chest, which is the right strategy for the hands they have. Slow the object down and the problem becomes solvable: a scarf falls at a speed she can think inside. Every catch she makes with the scarf is practice for the ball, and an early success at a physical skill keeps her with it long enough to get good at it.

days.safety: Balloons are the most dangerous choking hazard in the house for both of them, burst pieces and uninflated ones alike. Use the scarf instead any time Kreston is on the floor, count the balloons in and out, and throw away every scrap of a popped one the moment it goes.
